about: The Integrated Electrical Project is Part IA coursework in Cambridge's Engineering Tripos, done in your own space with an electronics kit issued towards the start of term: you build circuits through a series of exercises and upload findings to Moodle, alongside the Physical Principles of Electronics and Analysis of Circuits lectures. The 2026–27 credit notice gives 17 marks for its experiments (qualifying mark 15) and 12 for a final design project (qualifying mark 6) under the standard credit system. This is a guide to how it works and how to prepare; it has no exam syllabus of its own.

notes.h: What the Integrated Electrical Project is
notes.body:
The Integrated Electrical Project (IEP) is a piece of Part IA coursework in the Cambridge Engineering Tripos. It is not a lecture course with an exam syllabus, so this guide explains how it is organised and how to get the most out of it rather than setting out "topics" to revise.

What the Department's Part IA guide says about it
The guide is published on the 2026–27 teaching site, but its footer says it was last updated in September 2022, so details of how the IEP is run may have changed. The 2026–27 credit notice (next note) is current; check Moodle and the lectures for this year's arrangements.
- Unlike most Part IA experiments, it is not done in the teaching labs. You work in your own space.
- You are issued with an electronics kit towards the start of term.
- You work through a series of exercises in which you build circuits, make measurements and upload your findings to Moodle.
- It runs in parallel with two lecture courses: Physical Principles of Electronics (the first half of 1P3) and Analysis of Circuits. The idea is that what you see on the breadboard illustrates what you meet in lectures, and vice versa.
- The Part IA guide links it with the Exposition course, which develops writing and presentation skills. The guide says students' lab reports on an electronic filters experiment are critically reviewed in Exposition sessions, so expect your written work on circuits to be read and discussed.
- The guide says full instructions are given in the associated lectures, and the handouts are on Moodle. Treat those as the authority on deadlines and what to submit.

Where it sits in the year
- The 2026–27 coursework credit notice lists the IEP under Michaelmas and Lent terms.
- It has two parts for credit purposes: a set of experiments (short and long) and a final design project. The marks are covered in the next note.

How it connects to the exams
The IEP itself is coursework, but the ideas it exercises are examined in Paper 3 (Electrical and Information Engineering), which covers Physical Principles of Electronics and Electromagnetics, Analysis of Circuits and Devices and Digital Circuits and Information Processing. Building and measuring real circuits is one of the best ways to make Paper 3 material stick: you see that a capacitor really does pass high frequencies, that real components have tolerances, and that a measurement is only as good as the way it is taken.

What the IEP is not
- It is not a replacement for the examples papers. Do those as well.
- It is not marked on how elegant your circuit looks; it is marked on completing the exercises to the required standard and on the final design project, as set out in the credit notice.

Exam tips: the IEP has no exam, but keep your circuit sketches and measured results; they make excellent revision examples for Paper 3 questions on RC circuits, reactance and filters.

Cambridge Part IA coursework uses a "standard credit" system. Understanding it saves a lot of worry.

The figures below are from the Faculty Board's Part IA Coursework and Examination Credit Notice for 2026–27 (Tripos examinations in 2027). Always check the current notice on the teaching website, because figures can change from year to year.

IEP marks in 2026–27
- Experiments (Michaelmas and Lent): 3 short experiments at 2 marks each, 2 short experiments at 3 marks each and 1 long experiment at 5 marks. That is 6 + 6 + 5 = 17 marks available, with a qualifying mark of 15.
- Final design project: 12 marks available, with a qualifying mark of 6.

What "standard credit" means
- Once you reach a satisfactory standard in a group of activities, your marks for that group are capped at the qualifying level. In other words, going above the qualifying mark does not earn extra Tripos marks.
- If you fall short of the qualifying mark, or fail to attend or hand in required work, the shortfall is deducted from your Tripos total.
- The Department says the scheme is meant to reward punctual attendance, finishing work to a satisfactory standard and handing it in on time, and to stop students spending excessive time on any one activity. It also lets you try an ambitious design without a large penalty if it does not fully work.
- Most students are expected to reach the qualifying standard.

How coursework fits the overall Part IA mark (2026–27 notice)
- Each of the four written papers is marked out of 200.
- Coursework is worth 100 marks: the maximum raw coursework total is 200, and the final coursework mark is the raw total minus 100.
- The Part IA total is therefore 4 × 200 + 100 = 900 marks, so coursework is one ninth of the total. The Department's course overview also describes experimental work as 1/9 of Part IA credit.

Practical consequences
- The IEP experiments have a high qualifying mark (15 out of 17), so you cannot afford to skip or half-finish exercises. Missing even one 3-mark short experiment would put you below the threshold.
- The design project has a lower qualifying mark (6 out of 12), which leaves room for a design that is ambitious but imperfect.
- Deadlines matter. The Part IA guide sets out lateness penalties and a procedure for rearranging work you miss for reasons outside your control; speak to your Director of Studies or Tutor early if something goes wrong.

Exam tips: aim to secure the qualifying marks with no drama; time beyond that is better spent on Paper 3 examples papers.

notes.h: Working well on the IEP: preparation and background theory
notes.body:
Because you work on the IEP in your own room rather than in a staffed lab, organisation is half the battle.

Before each exercise
- Read the Moodle handout fully before you touch the kit. Note what you are asked to upload and in what form.
- Check the relevant lecture notes. The IEP runs alongside Physical Principles of Electronics and Analysis of Circuits, so the theory you need has usually just been lectured.
- Predict what you expect to measure. A quick calculation (a time constant, a cut-off frequency, a gain) lets you spot wiring mistakes immediately.

While building
- Lay the breadboard out neatly so it matches your circuit diagram; most faults are wiring faults.
- Check component values before inserting them (resistor colour codes, capacitor markings) and remember that real components have tolerances.
- Record measurements as you go, in tables with units, and plot graphs early so that anything odd shows up while you can still re-measure.

Background theory (general background, not IEP course content)
The list below is not taken from the IEP handouts, which define the actual exercises. It is standard circuit theory from the Paper 3 lecture courses that is likely to be useful whatever the exact exercises are.
- Ohm's law V = IR; resistors in series add; in parallel the reciprocals add.
- A capacitor obeys i = C dv/dt. With sinusoids its impedance is 1/(jωC), so its reactance 1/(ωC) falls as frequency rises. Current leads voltage by 90°.
- An inductor obeys v = L di/dt, impedance jωL; current lags voltage by 90°.
- An RC circuit charging from a step input has time constant τ = RC; it reaches about 63% of its final value after one time constant.
- A first-order RC low-pass filter (output across C) has gain 1/√(1 + (ω/ωc)²) with ωc = 1/(RC), so the cut-off frequency is fc = 1/(2πRC). At fc the gain is 1/√2 (−3 dB) and the phase shift is −45°. Well above fc the gain falls by a factor of 10 per decade of frequency (−20 dB/decade).
- Swapping R and C (output across R) gives a high-pass filter with the same fc.

Worked example
R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF give fc = 1/(2π × 1000 × 100 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 1.59 kHz. At 10 kHz the low-pass gain is 1/√(1 + (10/1.59)²) ≈ 0.157, with a phase lag of about 81°.

Writing up
- Say what you did, what you expected, what you measured and why they differ (tolerances, instrument loading, assumptions).
- Exposition sessions review filters reports critically, so clear graphs with labelled axes and units are worth the effort.

Exam tips: practise turning your IEP measurements into Paper 3 style calculations; examiners like candidates who can explain why a real circuit departs from the ideal.

questions.q: Under the 2026–27 Part IA credit notice, what happens if a student scores 13 out of 17 on the IEP experiments (qualifying mark 15)?
options: Nothing, provided the final design project is passed
The 2-mark shortfall is deducted from the student's Tripos total
The student must repeat Part IA
The 13 marks are added as bonus coursework credit
questions.why: Under standard credit, falling short of a qualifying mark means the shortfall is deducted from the Tripos total. The experiments and design project are separate rows with separate qualifying marks, so passing one does not cover the other; there is no automatic repeat of the year; and marks above or below qualifying are not bonus credit.

questions.q: An RC low-pass filter uses R = 2.2 kΩ and C = 47 nF. What is its cut-off frequency, to 2 significant figures?
questions.why: fc = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 2200 × 47 × 10⁻⁹) = 1/(6.50 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1540 Hz ≈ 1.5 kHz. 9.7 kHz is ωc = 1/(RC), about 9670 rad/s, mistaken for hertz; 240 Hz divides by 2π twice; 9.7 Hz is ωc with a factor-of-1000 slip in the units.

questions.q: A first-order RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Find its cut-off frequency, and the magnitude of its gain and its phase shift at 10 kHz.
markScheme: At 10 kHz, f/fc ≈ 6.28, giving gain ≈ 0.157 (about −16 dB)
questions.modelAnswer: The cut-off frequency is fc = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 1000 × 100 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 1590 Hz. The transfer function is H = 1/(1 + jωRC) = 1/(1 + j f/fc), so |H| = 1/√(1 + (f/fc)²) and the phase is −arctan(f/fc). At 10 kHz, f/fc = 10 000/1591.5 ≈ 6.28, so |H| = 1/√(1 + 39.5) ≈ 0.157 (about −16 dB) and the phase is −arctan(6.28) ≈ −81°: the output lags the input by about 81°.
